title: Using Random Forests for the Estimation of Multiple Users’ Visual Focus of Attention from Head Pose

fields.value: Technical system evaluation with single-user and two-user experiments.

quotes.text: The system has been tested both on single users and on couples of users interacting with a simple scenario designed to guide the user attention towards a specific space region.
The system has been tested on both single users and couple of users interacting within the same scenario.

fields.value: Controlled indoor setup in front of a television with a Kinect camera.

quotes.text: The user is positioned in front of a 47 in. smart TV with a resolution of 1920 1080 px. A Microsoft Kinect camera is located on top of the monitor.
The system has been tested in a simple scenario, where one or more users are placed in front of a smart TV endowed with a Kinect camera at a distance of 1.3 meters.

fields.value: 18 participants; arranged into 14 two-person couples for multi-user tests.

quotes.text: 18 users have been considered for the individual tests.

fields.value: 18 participants: 14 males and 4 females. Age and prior robot experience are not stated.

fields.value: Participants followed images appearing for four seconds in randomly selected regions of a six-quadrant television screen; they were asked to look at each image. In two-person sessions, both participants did this task simultaneously after sequential calibration.

quotes.text: The monitor shows a sequence of 10 different images located in one of the six different screen regions, randomly selected. Each image is shown for 4 s. The user is requested to look at the currently displayed image.
Thus, both users of the selected pair have been asked to look at each of the ten images randomly displayed on the screen.

fields.value: One human in single-user sessions; two humans in multi-user sessions. No robot was present in the interaction group.

fields.value: Kinect RGB-D sensor with OpenNI skeleton tracking and DRRF head-pose/VFOA estimation; screen-region hit and miss counts over each four-second image display, summarized as precision (also sensitivity in this setup).

quotes.text: Here, we adopted an approach that combines OpenNi standard functions for user tracking based on skeleton data gathered by the Kinect sensor, and a random forest method trained on the set of depth images.
For each user, the VFOA coordinates, as computed by the system, were compared to the position of the image displayed on the screen and observed by the user.

HIT COUNT: counts the number of times the coordinates of the focus calculated are recognized within the quadrant that contains the showed image; MISS COUNT: counts the number of times the coordinates of the focus computed by the system are localized outside such quadrant.

In order to evaluate the performance of our system, we considered the Positive Predictive Values (i.e., the Precision P TP/(TP FP)). In our case, since FP FN, this performance value identifies also the Sensitivity of the system.

fields.value: Mean precision was 0.82 for single users, 0.62 for individual users tracked in two-person sessions, and 0.39 when both users had to be correctly recognized at the same time. Single-versus-multiple-user precision differed significantly (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.0157); simultaneous joint attention recognition was described as unattainable in this setup.

quotes.text: For these tests, the achieved average Precision is 0.82.

With respect to the single user case, the performance, while tracking two users simultaneously, is degraded. One-way ANOVA test on Precision values of single users and multiple users test shows a significant difference in the two cases (with p 0.0157).
This means that, while two users’ VFOA can be tracked with a loss in performance, joint attention on a specific area is unattainable.

fields.value: The paper frames the topic as estimation of multiple users’ visual focus of attention (VFOA) from head pose, or head gaze, in multiparty interaction.

quotes.text: This work aims at evaluating the possibility of computing real-time multiple users’ focus of attention by combining a random forest approach for head pose estimation with the user’s head joint tracking.

fields.value: The paper treats VFOA as a person's focus of attention estimated from head pose; it does not provide a formal definition of robotic gaze, robotic attention, or robotic gaze-based attention.

quotes.text: This work aims at evaluating the possibility of computing real-time multiple users’ focus of attention, by combining the skeleton tracking of an RGB-D camera with the Random Regression Forest approach (DRRF) developed by [13] for the case of head pose estimation.
In order to determine the VFOA of a human user, we only considered the head pose estimation.

fields.value: The paper describes head gaze/VFOA as a social cue that can signal attention to a person or object, regulate turn-taking, inform whether to initiate interaction, and help estimate user engagement. These roles are discussed as motivation rather than tested with a robot.

quotes.text: Head gaze can hence be interpreted as an explicit social cue communicating attention towards a subject or an object, but also, it is used to regulate the turn-taking [9], to decide whether or not to initiate an interaction [10], as well as to estimate the degree of user’s engagement during a multi-party interaction [11].

fields.value: The system's VFOA estimation performance declined when tracking two users compared with one; jointly recognizing both users' attention to a screen region was poor. The study did not measure effects of a robot's gaze behavior on people.

fields.value: Autonomous estimation combines Kinect RGB-D depth images with OpenNI skeleton tracking and a Discriminative Random Regression Forest (DRRF) to identify heads and estimate nose position and Euler head-rotation angles. The estimated head pose is mapped to tracked users and projected onto a vertical plane to calculate VFOA.

quotes.text: Here, we adopted an approach that combines OpenNi standard functions for user tracking based on skeleton data gathered by the Kinect sensor, and a random forest method trained on the set of depth images.

fields.value: The paper evaluated a Kinect-based system that estimates one or two people's visual focus of attention from head pose while they looked at images on a screen. Precision fell from 0.82 with one user to 0.62 when tracking two users, and to 0.39 when both users had to be correct simultaneously; the study did not test a robot's gaze behavior.

RQ1; RQ2; RQ4; RQ5 — The paper describes head gaze/VFOA as a social cue and lists its possible roles in multiparty interaction, and details a real-time head-pose estimation system tested with one or two people. It uses a Kinect sensor rather than a robot embodiment, so it does not provide evidence about how a robot body influences gaze-based attention.
